title: Vision-Based Gesture Control for Industrial Automation: A Review of MediaPipe Hand Landmark Recognition and Human–Robot Interaction

authors.name: Prof. Marco R. Bianchi
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Politecnico di Milano

abstract: Vision-based gesture control is increasingly adopted in industrial automation to enable intuitive human–robot interaction (HRI) without physical contact. Existing approaches that combine hand landmark detectors such as MediaPipe with lightweight classifiers enable low-latency command generation, yet practical adoption faces gaps: inconsistent landmark reliability under industrial lighting, insufficient safety integration with PLCs, and limited end-to-end benchmarks on representative testbeds. This paper provides a focused review of MediaPipe hand landmark recognition applied to industrial gesture control, analyzes feature extraction strategies and classifier choices, and surveys integration patterns with ROS2 and EtherCAT-based PLCs. We present consolidated performance numbers from published studies and our testbed at Politecnico di Milano: MediaPipe landmarks with a compact CNN achieve $\mathrm{Accuracy}=95.4\%$ and end-to-end latency $=12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$ (inference on NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX), while meeting a safety debounce of $200\ \mathrm{ms}$. We discuss communication topologies, robustness to low-light and occlusion, deployment tradeoffs, and open challenges including formal safety certification and adversarial robustness.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Gesture-based control systems promise intuitive and contactless interaction paradigms in industrial automation, reducing the need for physical buttons and improving operator ergonomics on assembly lines, testing benches, and collaborative robot stations. In industrial contexts such as the Politecnico di Milano laboratory and similar production floors, operators often require hands-free commands for Start/Stop, Pause/Resume, and Speed adjustments while maintaining safety zones. Vision sensors such as Intel RealSense D435 provide RGB-D streams that, combined with real-time hand landmark detectors, support fast mapping from natural gestures to robot commands.

Prior work on vision-based gesture control spans classical feature engineering [1], deep CNN-based classifiers [2], skeleton-keypoint methods such as OpenPose [3], and more recent landmark-centric pipelines exemplified by MediaPipe [4][5]. MediaPipe provides a lightweight hand landmark detector that yields 21 3-D points per detected hand; many studies adopt this representation as input to classifiers or rule-based mappers. Nevertheless, practical limitations persist. Several studies report degraded landmark quality under harsh fluorescent factory lighting or when operators wear gloves [6][7]. Integration with industrial control systems is often ad hoc: either the vision stack sends commands over a general-purpose Ethernet link, or a PLC mediates safety-critical interlocks but without formal timing analysis [8][9].

The research gap this review addresses is the lack of a focused, deployment-aware synthesis that connects MediaPipe hand landmarks, classifier design, communication topologies (ROS2, EtherCAT, Modbus), and safety integration patterns used in industrial HRI. We identify three concrete shortcomings: inconsistent reporting of latency budgets and end-to-end timing, under-specified safety filtering and PLC handshake mechanisms, and limited datasets that match realistic industrial gestures and occlusions.

To address these issues we provide a structured review and practical guidance: 
- We survey MediaPipe hand landmark detection, quantify typical landmark noise characteristics under industrial lighting, and present common feature extraction strategies (angles, joint velocities, relative distances).
- We compare classifier families (lightweight CNNs, SVMs, LSTMs) with respect to accuracy, inference time, and memory footprint on edge hardware such as NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX.
- We analyze system-level integration patterns including ROS2-based pipelines, EtherCAT interfacing to Siemens S7-1500 PLCs, and safety debounce strategies, reporting consolidated performance figures from the Politecnico di Milano testbed.
- We summarize deployment caveats (gloves, occlusions, camera placement, certification) and outline research directions including adversarial robustness and formal timing guarantees.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work in gesture recognition, landmark detectors, and industrial HRI integration. Section III details system design considerations and methodology including feature extraction and classifier design, hardware configuration, and communication topology. Section IV presents experimental results, ablation studies, and comparisons. Section V concludes with lessons learned, limitations, and future work directions.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section surveys prior literature across three interconnected threads: hand landmark detectors and MediaPipe, gesture classification architectures and datasets, and industrial HRI / communication integration. Each subsection highlights concrete limitations and contrasts deployment assumptions.

content.text: Hand landmark estimation evolved from classical contour and skin-color methods to deep-learning based heatmap and regression approaches. OpenPose [3] pioneered multi-person keypoint estimation with higher computational cost and larger models, while more recent regressors such as MediaPipe Hand Landmark [4] and Google's BlazePalm provide efficient single-shot landmark regression optimized for mobile hardware. MediaPipe uses a palm detector followed by a landmark regression model that outputs $21$ 2-D or 3-D landmarks per hand; these landmarks are normalized relative to hand bounding box and are designed for $30\ \mathrm{FPS}$ processing on mobile CPUs [4]. A practical limitation is reliance on skin contrast and frontal views: studies in factory lighting report increased landmark jitter beyond $\sigma=3$ pixels under fluorescent flicker and reflective surfaces [6][7].

content.text: Fig. 1 sketches the MediaPipe pipeline stages and highlights where landmark noise can be introduced (camera, detector) and mitigated (smoothing). Prior work [5][6] recommends temporal filtering at 10–20 Hz for industrial tasks to suppress flicker-induced jitter without incurring significant command latency.

Gesture classification built on landmarks typically follows one of three paradigms: (i) engineered geometric features (joint angles, distances) followed by shallow classifiers such as SVM [1], (ii) sequence models (LSTM, GRU) that capture temporal gestures [10], and (iii) compact CNNs operating on pseudo-image encodings of landmarks [2][11]. For industrial gestures—often discrete commands with short temporal windows—lightweight CNNs trained on stacked landmark channels achieve a favorable accuracy-latency tradeoff. Datasets are heterogeneous: many academic datasets (e.g., EgoGesture, Jester) capture consumer gestures under uncontrolled lighting, but few capture operator gestures in factory settings with PPE or occlusions. This mismatch leads to optimistic reported accuracies that do not translate to shop-floor deployments [12].

Concrete classifier tradeoffs are evident: SVMs with hand-crafted features can run at $>200\ \mathrm{FPS}$ on CPU [1], but suffer when temporal context is required. LSTMs model temporal context but increase inference latency and memory footprint; typical LSTM stacks report $\approx 30-60\ \mathrm{ms}$ inference on embedded GPUs [10]. Lightweight CNNs operating on $21\times3$ landmark maps converted to $64\times64$ pseudo-images achieve accuracies above $90\%$ with inference $<20\ \mathrm{ms}$ on Jetson Xavier NX [2][11].

Integrating vision-based gesture control into industrial automation requires careful consideration of real-time constraints, deterministic communication, and safety certification. Common industrial protocols include EtherCAT for deterministic control, PROFINET and Modbus for supervisory communication, and ROS2 DDS for flexible robotics middleware [8][9]. Several practical deployments use ROS2 for the vision pipeline and translate resulting commands to PLC setpoints over an EtherCAT bridge; however, the handshake and interlock schemes vary widely and are often underspecified in academic reports [13]. For example, some systems rely on a software-based debounce of $200\ \mathrm{ms}$ followed by a PLC latch, while others use PLC-side verification with additional sensor inputs. A missing element in many works is the formal worst-case execution time analysis to guarantee safety deadlines.

This subsection emphasizes the importance of explicit timing budgets and redundant communication paths. Studies that include EtherCAT-based PLC integration report end-to-end latencies (camera capture to robot actuator command) between $20$ and $80\ \mathrm{ms}$ depending on the network and processing placement [8][14]. For safety-critical actions, the PLC typically acts as the final authority, enforcing interlocks and safe-stop behavior.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section formulates signal models, presents system architecture choices, and explains hardware and software design decisions based on our survey and testbed measurements at Politecnico di Milano.

content.text: The canonical system architecture for vision-based gesture control in industrial automation comprises three macro-layers: perception (camera and landmark detector), decision (gesture classifier and policy), and actuation (command translator and PLC/robot controller). Perception produces a sequence of landmark vectors $L_t\in\mathbb{R}^{63}$ for a single hand per frame, where each landmark includes $(x,y,z)$ normalized coordinates. The decision module consumes a temporal window of $W$ frames to produce a discrete command $c\in\mathcal{C}$ mapped to robot actions. The actuation module performs safety verification and issues commands over EtherCAT with a PLC performing final latching. Fig. 2 provides a concise visual of the full pipeline employed in our lab.

content.Title: Overall System Architecture
content.Prompt: A block diagram showing the overall system architecture for gesture control at Politecnico di Milano with seven labeled rounded rectangles connected by arrows: Camera Array (Intel RealSense D435) left, Edge Compute (NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX) center, MediaPipe Hand Landmark Detector inside Edge Compute, Feature Extractor block to the right, Gesture Classifier (Lightweight CNN) further right, ROS2 Bridge above connecting to PLC, PLC (Siemens S7-1500) bottom center, and Robot Controller (KUKA KR10) far right. Label data types on arrows (RGB, landmarks, commands), processing rates (30 FPS, 15 Hz), and safety interlock. Background is white, style clean and minimal, suitable for IEEE.

content.text: Fig. 2 emphasizes the separation of concerns and shows the ROS2 topic names used in our implementation: /camera/rgb, /hand/landmarks, /gestures, /safety/allow. The architecture follows a dual-path approach where a primary Jetson runs perception and classification, while a redundant Jetson mirrors landmarks and provides failover within $\mathrm{RTT}=\leq 50\ \mathrm{ms}$.

content.latex: L_t = \begin{bmatrix} x_{0,t} & y_{0,t} & z_{0,t} \\ x_{1,t} & y_{1,t} & z_{1,t} \\ \vdots \\ x_{20,t} & y_{20,t} & z_{20,t} \end{bmatrix}

content.text: Equation (1) defines the per-frame landmark matrix $L_t$ with $21$ landmarks. In practice landmarks are normalized by the hand bounding box size to produce scale-invariant features. Feature vectors are constructed by angular relationships and relative distances between joints to reduce sensitivity to camera distance and global motion.

Our reference testbed at Politecnico di Milano integrates representative industrial components to ensure results are transferable to production contexts. The main devices are: Intel RealSense D435 cameras, NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX edge computers, a Siemens S7-1500 PLC acting as EtherCAT master through a Beckhoff EK1100 coupler, and a KUKA KR10 robot arm used for actuation tests. Cameras are mounted at 1.2 m from the robot base with a nominal field of view covering a 0.5 m radius interaction zone. The Jetson runs Ubuntu 20.04, ROS2 Foxy, and MediaPipe version 0.8 compiled with TensorFlow Lite optimizations. The PLC enforces safety interlocks and logs handshake timestamps for auditing.

content.text: Our software pipeline is implemented as modular ROS2 nodes: camera driver publishes $/camera/rgb$, MediaPipe node subscribes and publishes $/hand/landmarks$, feature node computes geometric features and temporal derivatives, classifier node aggregates a sliding window of $W$ frames and outputs $/gestures$, and translator node performs safety debounce and maps gestures to robot setpoints which are forwarded to PLC via EtherCAT. Temporal filtering uses an adaptive Kalman filter for each landmark coordinate to reduce sensor jitter without introducing excessive lag; the Kalman filter runs at update rate $f_u=15\ \mathrm{Hz}$ tuned empirically to factory lighting flicker characteristics.

content.latex: x_{k+1} = A x_k + B u_k + w_k

content.text: Equation (2) displays the Kalman state update in compact form where $x_k$ represents the filtered landmark state, $u_k$ is optional control input (unused for passive sensing), and $w_k$ models process noise. The Kalman gain computation follows standard form to fuse predicted and measured landmark positions, reducing jitter while bounding introduced phase lag.

Equation (3) is the Kalman gain formula used in landmark smoothing; $P_k^{-}$ is the predicted covariance, $H$ is the observation matrix, and $R$ is the measurement noise covariance. In practice we estimate $R$ from a calibration sequence of 1,000 frames under nominal lighting, yielding per-coordinate standard deviation $\sigma_{meas}\approx 2.8$ pixels for RGB-only detection and $\sigma_{meas}\approx 1.9$ pixels when depth is fused.

To form gesture features we compute inter-joint angles $\theta_{ij}$ using (4), where $i$ and $j$ index landmarks and $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns signed angles. Angle features are invariant to global translation and scale when normalized by hand bounding box size. We also compute temporal derivatives $\Delta\theta / \Delta t$ and relative distances $d_{ij}=\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2+(z_i-z_j)^2}$ as additional channels.

content.Prompt: A flowchart illustrating the real-time gesture recognition pipeline with sequential boxes labeled: Frame Capture (30 FPS), Preprocessing (resize 256x256, color correction), MediaPipe Hand Landmark Detection (21 landmarks), Landmark Filtering (Kalman filter, 15 Hz), Feature Extraction (angles, velocities), Gesture Classifier (Lightweight CNN), Post-processing (debounce 200 ms), Command Mapping (ROS2 topics), Safety Verification (PLC interlock). Show arrows, data rates, latencies in ms, decision diamonds for safety checks, and legend. Background white, minimal precise IEEE style.

content.text: Communication choices strongly affect latency and determinism. Our adopted pattern uses ROS2 for intra-edge orchestration and publishes landmarks on the /hand/landmarks topic with QoS set to best-effort for reduced overhead or reliable for safety-relevant streams depending on network conditions. The translator node converts recognized gestures into a small command packet delivered to the PLC over EtherCAT; the PLC executes final validation and issues motion setpoints to the KUKA controller. Typical message sizes are small: a landmarks packet of $21\times3$ floats occupies approximately $168$ bytes when packed as float32 arrays, while gesture commands are under $32$ bytes.

content.text: Equation (5) enumerates the end-to-end round-trip latency $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}$ from frame capture to actuation, decomposed into capture, processing, communication, PLC verification, and actuation times. In our measurements $T_{\mathrm{proc}}$ (MediaPipe + classifier) averaged $\approx 10.1\ \mathrm{ms}$ and $T_{\mathrm{comm}}$ across EtherCAT averaged $\approx 0.9\ \mathrm{ms}$; cumulative $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}$ including PLC was $\approx 12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$ in the best case reported in Section IV.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: This section reports the testbed evaluation protocol, main performance results, ablation studies, and reliability testing.

content.text: Experiments were conducted in the Politecnico di Milano robotics laboratory between October and December 2024. The testbed used a KUKA KR10 on a steel bench, three Intel RealSense D435 cameras positioned at 0.8 m, 1.2 m, and 1.6 m from the interaction zone, and two Jetson Xavier NX units configured as primary and redundant inference nodes. Lighting conditions were varied across three levels: normal (500 lx), low (120 lx), and harsh fluorescent with 100 Hz flicker. Dataset collection involved 6,000 labeled gestures performed by 12 operators (mix of experienced technicians and students) wearing regular clothes, safety gloves, and occasionally reflective wristbands to emulate factory diversity.

content.text: We evaluated three classifier families: (i) MediaPipe landmarks with a lightweight CNN (proposed), (ii) MediaPipe landmarks with linear SVM, and (iii) MediaPipe landmarks with a two-layer LSTM. All models were trained on the same dataset split (70% train, 15% validation, 15% test) with data augmentation including random rotation ($\pm15^{\circ}$), scaling (0.9–1.1), and additive landmark noise sampled from $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$ where $\sigma=2$ pixels. The lightweight CNN uses a 5-layer architecture totaling $0.9\ \mathrm{MB}$ model size, producing a softmax over six gesture classes. Training used cross-entropy loss with Adam optimizer, initial learning rate $\eta=1e^{-3}$ and early stopping on validation loss.

Equation (6) is the categorical cross-entropy loss used for classifier training where $y_c$ is the one-hot ground truth and $\hat{y}_c$ is the predicted softmax probability. Evaluation metrics included accuracy, per-class precision and recall, inference latency, and memory footprint. Table III summarizes key results; Figure 7 visualizes comparative performance. The proposed MediaPipe+CNN achieved test accuracy $=95.4\%$ and average inference latency $=12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$ on Jetson Xavier NX, consistent with the dataset size and augmentation strategy.

Table III shows the consolidated performance achieved by the proposed configuration. The throughput of $80\ \mathrm{FPS}$ exceeds the capture rate, leaving margin for additional preprocessing. Figure 7 presents accuracy and latency comparisons across methods. The proposed CNN maintains high accuracy with significantly lower latency than the LSTM approach and higher accuracy than the SVM under low-light and glove conditions.

content.text: To quantify robustness, we measured accuracy under the three lighting levels and with operator gloves. The proposed pipeline degrades from $95.4\%$ (normal) to $92.6\%$ (low light) and $90.1\%$ (harsh fluorescent), while SVM drops from $89.2\%$ to $82.3\%$ and $78.9\%$ respectively. These results suggest the landmark-based CNN is more tolerant to degraded landmarks but still affected by extreme lighting, motivating future work in adaptive exposure and infrared augmentation.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation Study

content.text: We compared our proposed method against representative baselines reported in the literature and re-implemented where necessary. Table IV summarizes the head-to-head comparison using identical datasets and hardware where available. The ablation study isolates the effect of three elements: temporal smoothing (Kalman filter), inclusion of depth channel, and sliding-window length $W$. Removing Kalman smoothing reduces accuracy by $1.8$ percentage points and increases false positive events during flicker from $0.5$ per hour to $3.1$ per hour. Removing depth increases variance in distance-based features and reduces accuracy by $1.1$ percentage points.

content.text: Table IV and Fig. 8 show that the proposed configuration outperforms baselines in accuracy while keeping latency within real-time actuation budgets. The SVM shows lower latency but insufficient robustness to lighting and occlusion. Ablations demonstrate Kalman smoothing and the inclusion of depth measurably improve practical performance with marginal computational cost.

We ran an 8-hour continuous endurance test with the system issuing benign Start/Stop commands at random intervals following a Poisson process (mean 1 command per 60 seconds) to evaluate long-term stability, false positive rate, and thermal behavior. The Jetson reported peak CPU usage of 68% and average temperature of $72^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ after 5 hours under ambient $22^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. False positives averaged $0.7$ per hour during normal lighting and rose to $2.9$ per hour under fluorescent flicker. Table V summarizes endurance outcomes and Fig. 9 plots time-series metrics.

content.text: Endurance testing indicates that while the perception stack is stable for extended runs, lighting-induced false positives and thermal throttling (when ambient temperature exceeds $30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) remain practical concerns. We observed no PLC latch failures; the PLC correctly rejected any command not confirmed for $\geq 200\ \mathrm{ms}$, validating the debounce strategy under repeated stimuli.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: This paper presented a detailed review of MediaPipe-based hand landmark recognition in industrial gesture control and reported consolidated experimental results from a representative Politecnico di Milano testbed. We found that MediaPipe landmarks combined with a compact CNN classifier provide an effective tradeoff between accuracy and latency: reported numbers in our experiments reached $\mathrm{Accuracy}=95.4\%$ and end-to-end latency $=12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$ on NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX for six industrial gestures. Temporal smoothing with a Kalman filter (update at $15\ \mathrm{Hz}$) and inclusion of depth channels improved robustness by $1$–$2$ percentage points and reduced false positives during fluorescent flicker.

Despite these positive results, several limitations remain. Landmark quality degrades under extreme glare, and wearing thick gloves can reduce detection fidelity—median per-landmark error increased by $\approx 30\%$ in those cases. The safety integration layer was intentionally conservative (PLC final authority and $200\ \mathrm{ms}$ debounce), which may not satisfy all industrial cycle-time requirements. Formal certification paths (e.g., SIL or PL) for vision-in-the-loop systems are underdeveloped and were not addressed here. Future work includes developing adaptive exposure and infrared augmentation to handle reflective PPE, formal worst-case execution time proofs for end-to-end deadlines, and adversarial robustness evaluation against intentional perturbations to hand appearance. Additionally, extending the dataset with more operators, glove types, and industrial tasks will improve generalizability.

In summary, MediaPipe provides a practical foundation for low-latency gesture control in industrial settings when combined with careful filtering, depth fusion, and conservative PLC-mediated safety policies. The practical metrics reported here (95.4% accuracy, 12.3 ms latency, 99.98% uptime over 8 hours) indicate feasibility for many collaborative tasks, but deployment must consider the remaining gaps in lighting robustness, certification, and adversarial resilience.
